title: Structural Conditions for Distributed Quantum Advantage
authors: Sabina Drăgoi, María Gragera Garcés, Lirandë Pira
abstract: Circuit cutting runs a quantum computation on processors smaller than the circuit, at the price of classical knitting whose cost grows exponentially with the number of cut gates. Keeping this cost affordable is necessary but not sufficient for an advantage, since knitting classically easy subcircuits is itself classically easy. We formulate three requirements for distributed quantum advantage under a stated budget: affordable knitting, classical difficulty that survives the cut, and, for variational circuits, resolvable gradients. We prove that under stated assumptions knitting stays affordable when subcircuits grow behind a bounded interface and becomes exponentially expensive when fixed-width subcircuits multiply. We turn the requirements into screening criteria and apply them to eighteen circuit families. We identify finite local-depth circuits with bounded interfaces as a setting in which the requirements can coexist, with hardness established only in the worst case. As a classically verifiable proof of principle, we knit one gate joining two field-perturbed toric-code patches on an IBM Nighthawk processor for up to 142 spins, and confirm that the reconstruction can at least resolve the contact correlation beyond independent execution for up to 98 qubits.
summary: This paper establishes rigorous structural criteria—affordable classical knitting, preserved computational hardness, and stable gradients—required for distributed quantum advantage. By analyzing these criteria and testing them on toric-code patches on real hardware, the authors identify finite local-depth circuits as a viable path forward for modular quantum computation.
main_problem: The paper determines the structural conditions necessary to achieve a 'distributed quantum advantage' when running quantum computations across multiple, physically separated processors.
main_result: The authors identify Finite Local-Depth Circuits (FLDCs) with bounded interfaces as a promising architecture where the three necessary conditions—affordable knitting, classical hardness, and resolvable gradients—can coexist.
method: The methodology involves formulating three necessary screening criteria (Cut, Sim, Train) and applying them to various circuit families, supplemented by hardware experiments on toric-code patches.
model_or_system: The model is quantum computation distributed across multiple quantum chips, utilizing 'circuit cutting' to estimate expectation values from smaller subcircuits. The physical realization is tested on an IBM Nighthawk processor using field-perturbed toric-code patches.
key_observables: Knitting cost ($\Gamma_{cut}$), gradient variance ($	ext{Var}[\partial_\mu C]$), and contact correlation across the cut interface.
important_parameters: Bounded interface size, local depth ($\chi$), and the circuit size ($n$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the required hardness criterion ($S_1$) holds beyond the tested sizes, and the hardware results are limited by the one-parameter approximation used for signal correction.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate circuit cutting processes, the decay of gradient variance with causal distance, and the comparison of raw vs. rescaled device energies showing signal retention.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the three necessary criteria for distributed advantage (Cut, Sim, Train). It then analyzes these criteria across circuit families, proposing FLDCs as a solution. Finally, it validates this framework through both theoretical analysis of gradient decay and experimental testing on superconducting qubits.
why_interesting: The work directly addresses the practical limitations of scaling quantum computation by providing concrete, testable structural requirements for achieving advantage across modular hardware architectures.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

FIG. 3. A bounded interface leaves the affordable region only through the device width. The budget fixes a threshold κmax on the number of severed gates, independent of the circuit, while the circuit family fixes an interface curve κ∗(n), inde- pendent of the budget. The shaded region is both affordable and within device width. A bounded interface leaves it at nwidth, so hardware sets the reach. A growing interface leaves it through the budget threshold first unless the device width is reached earlier. The curves show minimum interfaces, whereas a heuristic search supplies upper bounds, and known gate angles should be assessed with the actual norm.
